Burnish

/BUR-nish/ - the stress falls on BUR · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Burnish means to polish, shine.

Before the auction, the estate's silver tea service was burnished until it doubled the candlelight.

Worked Example

The conservator drew a smooth agate stone across the saint's gold-leaf halo, burnishing it in tiny strokes for an hour until the dull metal woke up and shone like a coin.

Burnish is more exact than 'clean' or even 'polish' here: it names slow, patient rubbing that raises a deep shine on metal. Nothing was scrubbed off and nothing added — friction alone turned dullness into gleam, which is burnish's whole job.

How Burnish Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

polish

polish: the everyday word for making something shine

buff

buff: a quick, light rub-up, less patient than burnish

Antonyms

tarnish

tarnish: to let metal darken and dull

dull

dull: to take the shine away entirely

How Strong Is It? — wipe → polish → burnish

wipe vs. burnish

wipe vs. burnish: To wipe merely cleans — it stops far short of burnish, which works metal to a glow.

polish vs. burnish

polish vs. burnish: To polish goes further than wiping — it raises a shine — but stops short of burnish, which keeps rubbing until the metal holds a reflection.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — burn-

Root — burn-: brown (Old French brunir, 'to make brown, to polish' — English swapped the u and r on the way in)

Suffix — -ish

Suffix — -ish: verb-forming ending, as in finish and nourish

Put it together

Put it together: Burn- (brown — Old French brunir, 'to make brown, to polish'; English swapped the u and r on the way in) + -ish (verb ending) = to make brown. Polished metal glows a warm brown-gold in lamplight, so the metalworker's word for rubbing a surface until it shines came from 'browning' it — and English kept it as burnish.

Use the root in a new word: brunette

Use the root in a new word: brunette: The yearbook photo shows her as a brunette, years before the silver crept in.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Burnish is polish with patience and craft in it — metalwork, gold leaf, museum brass. Writers also borrow it figuratively: a candidate burnishes her image, a firm burnishes its reputation. For quick, casual shining, polish or buff is the plainer choice; if what you're adding is ornament rather than shine, that is adorn, not burnish.
